sources.title: Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference
sources.venue_or_author: Amy Yang, Jingyi Yang, Aya Ibrahim et al. (arXiv, v1 Nov 4 2024; v3 Apr 21 2025)
sources.summary: Shows that million-token prefill is a multi-node distributed-systems problem rather than an impossibility: ring-style context parallelism with pass-KV and pass-Q attention variants spreads a single 1M-token prompt across 128 H100 GPUs in 16 nodes and reaches 1M-context prefill of Llama3 405B in 77 seconds. The headline is that the bottleneck is time-to-first-token and GPU-seconds, not feasibility.
key_facts: 1M-token context prefill of Llama3 405B in 77s on up to 128 H100 GPUs across 16 nodes (arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783)
93% parallelization efficiency and 63% FLOPS utilization at 1M context (arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783)
128K-token context prefill in 3.8s on the same setup (arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783)
Introduces pass-KV and pass-Q ring attention variants for inference context parallelism (arxiv.org/abs/2411.01783)

sources.title: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving
sources.venue_or_author: Ruoyu Qin, Zheming Li, Weiran He, Mingxing Zhang et al., Moonshot AI + Tsinghua University (arXiv 2407.00079v4, Sep 3 2025; v1 2024)
sources.summary: Production serving architecture behind Kimi: prefill and decode run on separate clusters, and the KV cache lives in a disaggregated pool built from the CPU DRAM and SSD of the GPU servers, moved over RDMA. Long prompts are prefilled with chunked pipeline parallelism and layer-wise async KVCache transfer. Reported real-world effect: Kimi handles 75% more requests; simulations show 50%-525% throughput gains.
key_facts: Up to 525% throughput increase in certain simulated scenarios; 50%-525% depending on scenario (arxiv.org/html/2407.00079)
In real production, Mooncake lets Kimi handle 75% more requests (arxiv.org/html/2407.00079)
KVCache pool built from CPU DRAM and SSD of GPU nodes; 80GB HBM per A800 GPU; 800 Gbps RDMA interconnect (arxiv.org/html/2407.00079)
Chunked Pipeline Parallelism (CPP) and layer-wise prefill with asynchronous KVCache transfer for long contexts (arxiv.org/html/2407.00079)
Context lengths tested 16k, 32k, 64k, 128k; production trace avg input 7,590 tokens, avg output 182 tokens, 23,608 requests over 1 hour (arxiv.org/html/2407.00079)
Cache hit ratio of about 50% achievable with adequate storage; SLOs TTFT_P90 = 10x baseline, TBT_P90 = 5x baseline (arxiv.org/html/2407.00079)

sources.title: A Survey on Large Language Model Acceleration based on KV Cache Management
sources.venue_or_author: Haoyang Li, Yiming Li, Anxin Tian et al. (arXiv 2412.19442v3, Jul 30 2025)
sources.summary: Taxonomy of KV-cache optimizations at token level (selection/eviction, budget allocation, merging, quantization, low-rank), model level, and system level (memory management, scheduling, hardware-aware). Useful as the map of serving-time compression techniques (H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, KIVI, CacheGen, PyramidKV, InfiniGen, FlexGen) and gives the linear KV-growth formula that explains why long contexts are memory-bound.
key_facts: KV cache extra memory is O(L*h*t_o*(d_k+d_v)*sizeof(Float16)): linear in cached tokens x layers x heads x head dims (arxiv.org/html/2412.19442)
H2O keeps 'Heavy Hitter' tokens chosen by cumulative attention scores; SnapKV uses an observation window to score important tokens (arxiv.org/html/2412.19442)
StreamingLLM keeps initial 'attention sink' tokens plus recent context via the attention mask (arxiv.org/html/2412.19442)
KIVI quantizes keys per-channel and values per-token, keeping recent KVs in full precision; CacheGen uses layer-wise asymmetric quantization with delta encoding (arxiv.org/html/2412.19442)
PyramidKV allocates larger KV budgets to lower layers, shrinking upward; InfiniGen prefetches salient KV indices asynchronously; FlexGen uses per-token KV quantization (arxiv.org/html/2412.19442)

sources.title: Chain of Agents: Large language models collaborating on long-context tasks
sources.venue_or_author: Yusen Zhang and Ruoxi Sun, Google Research (Jan 23 2025)
sources.summary: Evidence for the 'distribute the problem instead of the window' answer: a chain of worker agents each reads a chunk and passes accumulated evidence forward, and a manager synthesizes the answer. With only 8k-token workers it beat both RAG and 200k-window full-context baselines on all eight datasets, with gains growing sharply beyond 400k input tokens. Also states why RAG fails (multi-hop first-hop chunks lack semantic similarity to the query) and why long windows fail (ineffective context utilization, quadratic cost).
key_facts: Up to 10% improvement over RAG and full-context baselines across all eight datasets (research.google blog, Jan 23 2025)
About 100% improvement when input exceeds 400k tokens (research.google blog)
CoA workers used 8k-token windows vs baselines at 8k and 200k tokens (research.google blog)
Evaluated on HotpotQA, MuSiQue, RepoBench-P, NarrativeQA, Qasper, QuALITY, QMSum, GovReport, BookSum with PaLM 2, Gemini Ultra, Claude 3 Haiku/Sonnet/Opus (research.google blog)
Paper link given in the post: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=LuCLf4BJsr (research.google blog)

sources.title: Introducing NVIDIA Dynamo, A Low-Latency Distributed Inference Framework for Scaling Reasoning AI Models
sources.venue_or_author: NVIDIA Developer Blog (Mar 18 2025)
sources.summary: NVIDIA's open inference framework formalizes the distributed answer: a planner splits GPUs between prefill and decode, a radix-tree smart router sends requests to the GPU already holding the matching KV prefix, a distributed KV cache manager offloads cold blocks to host memory, local storage, or networked object storage, and NIXL moves KV between devices over UCX/GDS/S3 backends.
key_facts: Up to 30x throughput for DeepSeek-R1 671B on GB200 NVL72 with Dynamo (developer.nvidia.com Dynamo blog, Mar 18 2025)
More than 2x throughput for Llama 70B on Hopper (developer.nvidia.com Dynamo blog)
Rationale: prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bound; use low tensor parallelism for prefill and high TP for decode (developer.nvidia.com Dynamo blog)
Smart Router tracks KV across GPUs with a Radix Tree and computes overlap scores to minimize recomputation (developer.nvidia.com Dynamo blog)
KV Cache Manager offloads less-used blocks to CPU host memory, local storage, or networked object storage; NIXL supports UCX, GDS, S3 backends (developer.nvidia.com Dynamo blog)

sources.title: Asking an Encyclopedia-Sized Question: How To Make the World Smarter with Multi-Million Token Real-Time Inference (Helix Parallelism)
sources.venue_or_author: NVIDIA Developer Blog (Jul 7 2025)
sources.summary: The clearest statement of the decode-side hardware bottleneck at million-token contexts: every generated token must stream the whole KV history from DRAM and re-load FFN weights, saturating memory bandwidth and raising token-to-token latency. Helix Parallelism shards attention (KV) and FFN differently in a temporal pipeline across NVL72 to raise concurrency at fixed latency.
key_facts: Two decode bottlenecks named: KV cache streaming from DRAM per sample and FFN weight loading per step (developer.nvidia.com Helix blog, Jul 7 2025)
Up to 32x more concurrent users at fixed latency and up to 1.5x lower minimum token-to-token latency (developer.nvidia.com Helix blog)
Tested at 1 million token context with DeepSeek-R1 671B, FP4, on a simulator calibrated to GB200 NVL72 (developer.nvidia.com Helix blog)
Helix Parallelism defined as a hybrid sharding strategy that disaggregates attention and FFN parallelism in a temporal pipeline (developer.nvidia.com Helix blog)

sources.title: DeepSpeed-Ulysses: System Optimizations for Enabling Training of Extreme Long Sequence Transformer Models (blog)
sources.venue_or_author: Microsoft DeepSpeed team
sources.summary: Training-side sequence parallelism: each sample is split along the sequence dimension across GPUs; an all-to-all before attention gives each GPU the full sequence for a subset of heads, and a second all-to-all re-partitions by sequence. Enables over 1M-token training and beats Megatron-LM sequence parallelism on length and communication, but notes that local quadratic attention still dominates at extreme lengths.
key_facts: Trains with over a million tokens of sequence length; 4x longer sequences than Megatron-LM SP (DeepSpeed-Ulysses README)
Over 10x communication reduction vs comparable approaches; 2.5x throughput, up to 175 TFLOPs/GPU (54% of peak) (DeepSpeed-Ulysses README)
Scalability test: 1.2B-parameter GPT at 1M tokens (DeepSpeed-Ulysses README)
Limitation: throughput primarily determined by local attention compute due to quadratic complexity for dense attention (DeepSpeed-Ulysses README)
Technical report: arXiv:2309.14509 (DeepSpeed-Ulysses README)

sources.title: DeepSpeed Ulysses: System Optimizations for Enabling Training of Extreme Long Sequence Transformer Models (paper)

sources.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM)
sources.venue_or_author: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng et al., SOSP 2023 (submitted Sep 12 2023)
sources.summary: Foundational serving-side KV memory management: the KV cache is stored in non-contiguous paged blocks like virtual memory, giving near-zero waste and enabling KV sharing across requests, which raised throughput 2-4x over FasterTransformer and Orca at equal latency. Basis for later prefix caching and KV offload work.
key_facts: vLLM improves throughput of popular LLMs by 2-4x at the same latency vs FasterTransformer and Orca (arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
PagedAttention achieves near-zero waste in KV cache memory (arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
Published at SOSP 2023; arXiv submission Sep 12 2023 (arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

sources.title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for KV cache eviction
sources.venue_or_author: Described in the 2025 KV-cache survey arXiv:2412.19442 (ref [131]); original paper year and URL not confirmed in this sweep
sources.summary: Serving-time KV eviction: keeps a small set of 'heavy hitter' tokens identified by cumulative attention scores plus recent tokens, shrinking the KV cache so longer contexts fit in HBM. Description taken from the survey; no direct fetch.

notes: BUDGET NOTE: WebSearch was already exhausted session-wide (200/200) before this sweep started, so zero searches ran; all evidence comes from 8 WebFetch calls on canonical URLs plus reference lists inside those pages. Coverage achieved: multi-node prefill (Meta context parallelism), training sequence parallelism (DeepSpeed-Ulysses vs Megatron SP), disaggregated prefill/decode and KV offload (Mooncake, NVIDIA Dynamo), decode hardware bottleneck at 1M+ tokens (NVIDIA Helix), paging/prefix reuse (vLLM, SGLang/Dynamo radix routing), KV compression taxonomy (survey: H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, KIVI, CacheGen, PyramidKV), and decomposition-over-window evidence (Chain-of-Agents). NOT COVERED due to budget: direct Ring Attention / Striped Attention papers, Megatron-Core context-parallel docs, LMCache, CacheBlend, MemGPT, TokenSkip, speculative decoding, and any 2026 model-window spec pages (GPT-5 default window, Claude/Gemini 1M) — the report should take those from other modalities. The four KV-compression entries with url=unknown are described only via the survey (their year field is the survey's year, not the original paper's). The Mooncake fetch mislabeled vLLM's arXiv ID (it gave the LLaMA-2 ID), which is why vLLM was fetched directly. SYSTEMS SYNTHESIS: (1) Prefill at 1M tokens is feasible but expensive: 77s on 128 H100s for a 405B model, i.e., roughly 2.7 GPU-hours per single 1M-token request, which is the TTFT/cost wall that makes providers cap or price long windows. (2) Decode at multi-million contexts is bounded by HBM bandwidth for streaming the KV history every step, not by FLOPs (Helix), so per-token latency degrades with context even when memory fits. (3) KV memory grows linearly per token x layers x heads (survey formula), so serving stacks page it (vLLM), share prefixes (RadixAttention, Dynamo router), spill it to DRAM/SSD/object storage over RDMA/NIXL (Mooncake, Dynamo), split prefill from decode onto different GPU pools (Mooncake +75% requests in production; Dynamo up to 30x on GB200 NVL72 for R1), chunk prefill (Sarathi), and compress/evict/quantize (H2O, SnapKV, KIVI). (4) The non-window answer has direct evidence: Chain-of-Agents with 8k-token workers beat both RAG and 200k full-context baselines on eight datasets, with ~100% gains above 400k input tokens, suggesting that beyond a few hundred thousand tokens, distributing the problem across agents can outperform widening the window.
